newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Renault warns of bigger losses, shares fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Renault warns of bigger losses, shares fall.

text.p: French carmaker Renault on Friday sounded a fresh warning about its 1996 results, saying its operating loss would be considerable higher than market expectations.
Shares in the company, which said previously it expected to lose money on both its car and truck operations and report its first annual loss in 10 years, closed 5.7 percent down at 122.50 francs.

Shares in other motor companies also fell on the latest gloomy pronouncements from the French car industry, which began the year on a grim note. PSA Peugeot Citroen shares closed 4.58 percent lower at 584 francs.

French car sales fell 34 percent in January, revealing the market's underlying weakness after more than two years of state support through incentives for people to buy new vehicles. The incentives ended last autumn.
"France is a pretty nasty place to try and sell cars," said one industry analyst.

Analysts had pencilled in an operating loss of between 1.3 billion francs ($229 million) and 1.6 billion francs for Renault, whose profit margins were eroded last year by a savage price war among carmakers fighting to boost their share of Europe's slow-growing market.

"In view of the prevailing economic context, and despite the increase in revenues of the automobile division...the operating loss to be reported by Renault Group for 1996 will be considerably higher than that generally anticipated by the financial markets," Renault said in its 1996 sales statement.
It said its performance last year was marred by "relentless and aggressive price wars", which drove up marketing costs, and lower truck sales in the United States where Renault owns Mack Trucks.

"The efforts made by the company in the area of cost reduction were not sufficient to offset the negative effects of a difficult price environment in Europe and the interruptions relating to the introduction of replacements in the company's product line," it said.
Its 1996 sales totalled 184.08 billion francs, almost unchanged from the previous year's sales of 184.07 billion as a 9.5 percent drop in truck sales offset a 2.3 percent gain in the car division.

Analysts said the biggest problem appeared to be in the car division, which has been losing money since the second half of 1995. Several said they are now looking for a division operating loss of around three billion francs, compared with prior estimates of a two billion franc loss and a 1995 operating loss of 1.7 billion francs.
"I don't think they'd have issued another profit warning unless the difference (with the market's estimate) was significant," said one analyst with a French bank.
The analyst said he thought Renault shares were cheap, given his expectations that its popular new Megane Scenic and Espace models would boost market share this year.
Currency shifts, notably the British pound's rise, would also help results and European consumer spending should improve, he added.
The effects of a cost-cutting drive put in place a year ago by Renault would kick in this year, he said.

Renault and its French rival PSA Peugeot Citroen appealed late last year to the government for assistance in carrying out a hefty early retirement programme to cut their costs and rejuvenate their workforces.

Industry Minister Franck Borotra said in an interview published in Friday's business newspaper Les Echos that the government had not reached a decision on the pleas. It would take into account "the challenges of global competitiveness and jobs for young people".

The French carmakers, ranked fifth and sixth in January among Europe's Big Six, will face even greater competition when European Union import quotas on Japanese vehicles are eliminated in the year 2000. ($ = 5.677 French Francs)
